newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank lashes call to amend EMU stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank lashes call to amend EMU stability pact.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Friday lashed out at calls for amendments to the stability pact on fiscal discipline by nations qualifying for European monetary union.

Fresh from thwarting Bonn's plans to draw on central bank reserves this year, senior bank officials said they expected the pact would be ratified in its current form and warned against attempts to soften it.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said in Duesseldorf he was "very irritated" by a reported move by the European parliament to push through amendments weakening the pact.
"That could also cause a lot of problems for the German government which has placed emphasis on the need for automatic sanctions," Jochimsen told a news conference.
Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said in Frankfurt he expected the pact to be ratified on schedule at the Amsterdam EU summit starting on June 16.

"I am working on the assumption that the current version stands and that the stability pact will be nailed down in its current form in Amsterdam," he told reporters at a conference sponsored by the German central bank.
The pact will impose sanctions on euro member nations exceeding the deficit ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

Agreed after tough negotiations between the Germans and the French at an EU summit in Dublin last December, it is seen as crucial to overcoming German doubts that the euro will be as stable as the mark.

Those doubts have gained ground in recent weeks following the election of a left-wing French government opposed to fiscal austerity measures and Bonn's attempt to seize part of the Bundesbank's gold reserves, which was widely condemned as a blatant accounting trick.

France's new government has indicated it is unhappy with the stability pact and may wish to reopen it. Also, the Financial Times reported on Friday that the European Parliament wanted to push through amendments weakening it.
Meanwhile Bundesbank officials said they would discuss a planned compromise on the revaluation its assets at the bank's next central council meeting on June 12.

Faced with tough resistance from the central bank, Bonn this week backed down from its plan to revalue the bank's reserves and transfer part of the profit to government coffers in 1997 to help Germany qualify for the euro.
Instead, the two sides have agreed to discuss the revaluation of certain Bundesbank assets at the end of 1997 with a possible payout in 1998.

Details of the planned compromise are sketchy but Jochimsen said he saw no scope for any profit transfer from a revaluation of the Bundesbank's gold reserves unless gold was sold -- a move both sides have firmly ruled out.

Jochimsen, who is also president of the state central bank of North Rhine-Westphalia, said he did, however, see room for a profit transfer resulting from a revaluation of the Bundesbank's currency reserves.

Separately, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing said in Frankfurt there was no reason to expect that monetary union would be delayed from its January 1999 start date but added that unemployment data for May created additional problems for Bonn's budget.
German unemployment rose 56,000 to a seasonally-adjusted 4.358 million people in May. The unemployment rate, based on unadjusted data, fell to 11.1 percent from 11.3 percent.
